articles.content: There is more American Horror Story in our future. The debut episode landed on Nielsen’s Streaming Top 10 charts and repped Murphy’s biggest launch ever on Hulu and Disney+. articles.content: “When I took this job, Bela gave me a simple piece of advice: Be yourself,” wrote Dan Lin in his exit email to Netflix staff, following the news on Monday that he will no longer serve as the streamer’s film chief. It was a fitting anecdote given that Dan Lin — the Harvard Business School grad turned studio executive turned movie producer behind hits like The Lego Movie and $1 billion grosser Aladdin who is known for his calculating and budget-conscious acumen — was hired to be Dan Lin. Bob Iger's New Book to Chronicle "Sometimes Bumpy, Never Boring" Second Stint as Disney CEO
articles.content: Former Disney CEO Bob Iger has officially announced his second book, and it will tackle his second run as CEO, according to publisher Penguin Random House. The book, One Last Time , will be released on March 2, 2027, with Dan Schwerin helping to write it. Per the publisher, the book “is the candid inside story of the sometimes bumpy, never boring journey to reconnect a great company to its core values, while building a new, lasting foundation in a rapidly changing world.” Among the topics that Iger will write about is taking back the reins of the company from former CEO Bob Chapek (who wrote a book of his own released earlier this month), but also everything that followed, from the rush of AI disruption to the suspension of Jimmy Kimmel. The two grueling proxy battles and the 2023 Hollywood strikes are also part of the story, the publisher says. “This is a comeback story,” Iger says in a statement. “It’s about what Disney needed to find its way back to its core values and what that journey taught me about leading in a time of unprecedented challenge and change.” The veteran executive staff stepped aside as CEO again earlier this year, handing control of the entertainment giant to Josh D’Amaro. He remains on Disney’s board, but is set to leave it at the end of the year. Iger wrote his first book , The Ride of a Lifetime , in 2019, capping off a long and successful run running The Walt Disney Co. He would end up passing the baton to Chapek just a few months after the book was released. But his new memoir will cap off a run of books about the company, and himself. Chapek made Iger a starring character in his own memoir, blaming him for undermining his leadership after selecting him for the top job. And later this year an unauthorized book by Wall Street Journal reporter Robbie Whelan will release a book promising to document the “Machiavellian power struggle” inside the company. In May, the New York Times reported that Prognosis: Negative, a long-lost script by Larry David had emerged on eBay. The story went viral, but what few knew at the time: author Blake J. An R-rated horror movie about a minor Batman villain, the film is the first true test of their thesis that DC Comics mythology is diverse and complex enough to support a wide range of films in completely different genres. Its creative team has some serious horror bona fides: the film was pitched by Mike Flanagan, who wrote the original script that remained largely intact after revisions by Hossein Amini; and directed by none other than James Watkins , whose filmography includes spooky hits like “The Woman in Black” and “Speak No Evil.” But most notable of all, perhaps, is the fact that “Clayface” gives us our first look at the DC Studios take on Gotham City. Directors ranging from Tim Burton to Christopher Nolan have each put their own distinct visual spin on the urban setting. And while Gunn and Safran have not announced a Batman of their own (the Matt Reeves/Robert Pattinson series is continuing , but exists separately from their interconnected universe), everyone knows it’s coming at some point. articles.summary: The late Washington Post critic was the rarity we should all aspire to be: a sharp observer and a deep mensch
articles.content: I don’t remember when I started working with Ann Hornaday . I mean, I know the date because I had an employment letter from HR. But I don’t recall a shift in how she related to me as I went from someone at a competing newspaper to a colleague inside the fold. She’d already treated me like I was part of her family. She already treated everyone like they were part of her family. So when I joined The Washington Post in 2017 from The Los Angeles Times , it brought no change in our dynamic. She just continued being as warm — and friendly and empathetic and commiserative — as when we worked apart. Ann didn’t have Jewish blood as far as I know. But with her, you were always mishpocha . Ann died on Sunday at age 66. Gone way too soon, but for a good soul, is there ever on time? I didn’t lead with the fact that she was a film critic — and a damn good one, as evidenced by her many viral reviews, her acclaimed book Talking Pictures and her finalist status for the Pulitzer Prize — because it wasn’t the most salient thing about her. The most salient thing about her was her clear-eyed view of the world — and how she treated you as if you were all of her world. I do remember the first day I met Ann. It was at the Cannes Film Festival in the early 2010s, at one of those anonymous townie apartments where talent interviews were being conducted. An OG indie-film publicist named Jeff Hill introduced us. “You guys know each other, right?” he said to me, I still feeling like a cub in the clubby world of Cannes journalists. I didn’t know her, and I was worried she was about to underscore that, in fact, she didn’t know me. But not missing a beat, she looked at both Jeff and myself. “Of course,” she said warmly. She knew we’d never met. But that was in the past. She knew me now, so why harp on anything else? articles.title: Nudity Banned from ‘Friday the 13th’ Reboot, Showrunner Says: “That’s America”
articles.summary: But tons of violence in Peacock's 'Crystal Lake' is perfectly fine, of course: "God forbid they see some breasts."
articles.content: The Friday the 13th movies are known for slasher horror violence and the occasional flashes of sex and nudity as randy camp counselors are stalked by a mysterious killer. But the showrunner behind Peacock’s TV series reboot of the iconic franchise says he was overruled when he tried to include nudity in the show. Crystal Lake showrunner Brad Caleb Kane was asked by The Wrap about the lack of skin in the series (there is apparently only a shot of a person’s backside in one scene). Related Stories TV 'Crystal Lake' Review: Peacock's Linda Cardellini-Starring Series Is the Best 'Friday the 13th' Property Yet (Which Isn't Saying a Lot) TV 'Crystal Lake' Will Offer More Brutal Kills Than Films, Go Deep on Jason's Background “I tried,” Kane said. “That’s America. You can give the kids the violence, but God forbid they see some breasts. Sometimes you get overruled in these things.” Indeed, the show is extremely violent and gory — perhaps even moreso than many of the films. The nudity in the movies, if one were to get analytical about these things, actually had a purpose beyond titillation. It’s the classic horror trope of the “sin” of sex leading to death, with voyeuristic nudity and the shock of the killing luring the viewer into guiltily experiencing this cycle. One can trace the trope back to Alfred Hitchcock’s famous shower scene in Psycho , and it extended through Friday the 13th and Halloween and countless other horror films. Kane doesn’t specify who overruled the nudity, but it seems highly unlikely it was the show’s production company A24, given it also makes shows like Euphoria . Peacock has occasionally had an original series with nudity (2020’s Brave New World , 2024’s Those About to Die ), but isn’t exactly known for being an edgy streamer.

The news of U2 playing the Netflix Thanksgiving Eve game comes as Puck reported that Jay-Z has booked himself for next year’s Super Bowl, which also be held at SoFi. Jay-Z’s Roc Nation is responsible for booking and producing the halftime show for the NFL.

articles.title: Versant CEO Says Buying Skydance Cable Networks Is ‘Probably Not in Our Short-Term Future’
articles.summary: Mark Lazarus dispels rumors that the NBCUniversal spinoff would acquire the merged company's linear assets The post Versant CEO Says Buying Skydance Cable Networks Is ‘Probably Not in Our Short-Term Future’ appeared first on TheWrap .
articles.content: Mark Lazarus dispels rumors that the NBCUniversal spinoff would acquire the merged company’s linear assets Versant CEO Mark Lazarus said that the company, which was spun off by Comcast and NBCUniversal earlier this year, is not interested in buying other cable networks. “Buying more cable assets on a large scale would prolong our life but not necessarily make our life better because we would still have the secular decline,” the CEO said Tuesday at the Axios Media Trends Live conference. “Might there be some interest in another vertical that we could create around a pay television business? Yes, but just buying big networks or a bunch of networks that don’t necessarily change our trajectory is probably not in our short-term future.” Versant took on a large chunk of NBCU’s cable networks in the spinoff, including networks such as MS NOW, CNBC, USA and Syfy. The company also manages digital properties, including Fandango and Golf Now. The CEO said the company is instead more focused on diversifying its revenue “in adjacent businesses that are incredibly powerful consumer branded networks as an amplifier and create bigger businesses,” like golf. Earlier this month, Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery merged to form Skydance and created a media giant with more than 50 cable networks. The company claimed that they are not interested in selling its networks but planned to pay down their debt and invest in other avenues. When asked specifically about Comcast’s plan to spin out NBCUniversal and whether Versant would ever consider reuniting with the media giant NBCU down the road, Lazarus did not answer straight on. “Our cash flow is really strong, and I think we will find our path, whether it’s on our own transformation or alongside someone else, but no, that wouldn’t be the plan to necessarily go back to them,” he said.

articles.title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Would Have Looked Much Different Without Emma Stone’s Help
articles.summary: Stone and Nathan Fielder previously worked together on "The Curse" The post ‘You Can See Everything’ Would Have Looked Much Different Without Emma Stone’s Help appeared first on TheWrap .
articles.content: “You Can See Everything” would have felt and looked very different without Emma Stone’s help. In a new interview with Vulture , director Lance Oppenheim recounted that getting (spoiler) Amanda Seyfried involved in the film wouldn’t have happened without Stone. At a little over the halfway point of the film, Nathan Fielder heads to Seyfried’s home to show her clips of his month living with Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes and her husband Billy. Things take a particularly uncomfortable turn when Seyfried is forced to watch clips of Holmes seeing “The Dropout” – the Hulu show where Seyfried played the Theranos founder during her rise and fall. All that and what came after was largely due to Stone. At the end of the film, the two-time Academy Award winner was mentioned in the Special Thanks section of the credits. Initially, most people assumed the help came because the actress and Fielder were friends and had previously worked together on the Showtime TV series “The Curse.” Oppenheim revealed that she actually helped set up the introduction between the filmmakers and Seyfried. Oppenheim said initially all he was hoping for was to show Seyfried the footage they shot and hope her reaction led to “a deeper understanding of what we’d made.” That changed when “The Dropout” star admitted to wanting to play Holmes again. From then on, the back half of the film becomes more more like Fielder’s HBO series “The Rehearsal” as Seyfried plays Holmes in a number of reenactments after the real woman is placed behind bars. “As soon as Elizabeth leaves, the movie is sort of haunted by her absence,” Oppenheim said. “Everyone in it is attempting to remember her in different ways and also create a version of her.” So if your favorite part of the movie was Seyfried’s involvement, her reenactments, or her reactions to Billy, go ahead and thank Stone.

articles.title: ‘Klara and the Sun’ Review: Jenna Ortega Plays a Manic Pixie Android in Taika Waititi’s Confoundingly Awful Kazuo Ishiguro Adaptation
articles.summary: Leave your brain behind. Where Ishiguro whisks you away with crisp, powerful prose in his celebrated dystopian fable, Waititi instead thwacks you with relentless whimsy and soul-crushing tweeness in an inadvertent(?) bid for director jail.
articles.content: Leave your brain at the door, lest you want your IQ pulverized, if you see Taika Waititi ’s confoundingly awful, relentlessly twee Kazuo Ishiguro adaptation, “ Klara and the Sun .” Starring Jenna Ortega as solar-powered AF (artificial friend) Klara, whose overexposure to broad, deeply stupid human feelings starts to empower her with them, it’s this year’s “ A Big Bold Beautiful Journey ” — another auteur-backed misfire and unintended preamble to director jail. Where Ishiguro, the Nobel-winning Japanese-British author of “The Remains of the Day” and “Never Let Me Go,” writes in plaintive, precise prose grounded in ambiguous emotions, Waititi fills in the spaces with pastel-popped set design, thwacks of whimsy, and gauche slapstick comedy that undermine every already-half-hearted gesture at profundity. Take a scene where two characters run to Klara’s rescue amid a burning building, only to get shocked by an electric fence at least three times, but more, I think. Michael Giacchino’s bathetic score, layered over such a bizarrely cued pratfall, crystallizes precisely the miscalculated clash of tensions felt in every frame as the movie supposedly hurtles toward a big emotional climax. “Klara and the Sun” is pathologically allergic to sincerity, treating major existential questions as treacle — and worse, uncuriously. articles.title: WGA East Moves to Block AI Models from Training on Members’ Work with New Software Partner Cloak: ‘Give Agency Back to Writers’
articles.summary: WGAE members can register scripts with the program for free, while non-members can for a $10 fee.
articles.content: The Writers Guild of America , East unveiled a partnership to help prevent AI models from training off of its members’ work on Tuesday. The software program Cloak, which creates copies of files that are illegible to AI models but readable for humans, will be available for free to WGAE members as part of the union’s benefits program. The encryption tool will protect writers from their work being exploited by AI without their consent. “The WGAE partnership with Cloak expands our efforts to protect members’ work and fight back against AI companies exploiting writers and other creative workers,” WGA East president Tom Fontana said in a statement unveiling the partnership. “Members don’t need to worry that their work will be used to train AI models after they send it to producers or agents — or simply that the product of weeks, months, or years of work will be reduced to an AI-generated summary of an email attachment.” Related Stories Ryan Gosling Turned Obstacles Into Opportunities on ‘Project Hail Mary’ — with a Little Help from Julia Roberts ‘Clayface’ Introduces DC Studios’ Gotham City — but Director James Watkins Never Felt Pressure to Set Up Future Films In addition to being provided as a free service to those within the WGAE, writers who aren’t members can add Cloak by registering their script through the guild’s website.
